claim: Traffic signals adapt through a distributed consensus mechanism where intersections negotiate timing adjustments based on shared traffic flow predictions.
mechanism: Each intersection maintains a local model of traffic flow and shares predictions with adjacent intersections. Through iterative negotiation, intersections agree on signal timing that optimizes for collective rather than individual performance. The consensus process uses weighted voting based on intersection importance and traffic volume.
evidence: Consensus algorithms work well in distributed systems
Negotiation-based approaches have succeeded in resource allocation problems
Traffic prediction models have shown reasonable accuracy in short time horizons
assumptions: Intersections can reliably share traffic predictions with neighbors
Negotiation process converges quickly enough for real-time adaptation
Local traffic models are sufficiently accurate for prediction
expected_failure_modes: Deadlock in consensus process during conflicting traffic conditions
Bias toward high-volume intersections at expense of overall network efficiency
novelty_rationale: Transfers the concept of distributed consensus from biological systems to traffic signal optimization, emphasizing collective decision-making over individual optimization.
testability: Can be tested by implementing a consensus protocol between simulated intersections and measuring the time to reach agreement and resulting traffic flow improvements.
falsifier: If the negotiation process fails to converge within the required 15-minute timeframe or results in significantly worse performance than centrally optimized signals, this hypothesis would be proven wrong.
